The AI chat app shows you a conversation. The model has no idea what that is.

The model sees a single block of text, rebuilt from scratch and sent in full every time you submit a message, and it forgets all of it the second the answer is sent.

The panel shows both sides: the chat interface you see, and what actually gets sent to the model.

You open a new chat with an assistant that can read your Drive and your inbox, and type “hi” .

hi

Before your message, the app puts a system prompt in front of it. That is where the instructions live, like who the assistant is and what it must never do.

A few thousand tokens usually, before your first message.

Then come the tools . Every action the assistant can take (search your Drive, edit a document or draft an email) is described in the request with a name, a description and a JSON schema telling the model how to call it.

The model can only call what it has been told exists, so all of that ships with every request.

Your “hi” is now the smallest thing in an 18,000-token prompt. Every connector you add makes it bigger whether it’s used or not.

Newer setups can hold tool definitions back until the model searches for them.

If you use Claude Code, /context shows you this breakdown for your own session.

The model replies with 11 tokens.

Output costs more per token, 4x-8x the input price on most models.

Hi! What are you working on today?

You send a second message.

The model has no memory of your first request.

Every turn, the app sends the entire conversation again: tools, system prompt, your “hi”, its reply, and then your new message at the bottom.

I need to write the Q3 operations report by Friday.

Do you have last quarter's report? I can follow its structure.

Every chat API works this way.

The conversation lives in the client, and each request carries the whole history.

The interface hides the line between what the model does and what the application around it handles for you.

Keep talking and each request is a little bigger than the one before.

You paste last quarter’s report, and it rides along on every request after that.

[pastes the Q2 report, 4 pages]

It has four sections: headcount, spend, incidents and next quarter's goals. I'd keep that order.

Start with headcount. We hired six and lost two.

Headcount: the team grew from 41 to 45, with six hires and two departures.

Less formal, it reads like a press release

Here's a plainer version: ...

Does the spend section need a chart?

One chart of spend by category, quarter over quarter. The rest fits in a table.

After 6 turns you have typed ~2,600 tokens, and the model has received ~120,000 tokens.

Every request pays again for everything before it, so that total grows with the square of the conversation’s length.

You ask the model a complex question, which triggers some reasoning .

The chat shows a collapsed “Thought for 21s” . That was 2,100 tokens of text the model wrote (to itself) before answering.

Why doesn't my travel total match the one finance sent?

Thought for 21s

Finance books travel when the invoice arrives. Your sheet uses the trip date, so three late-September trips are Q3 for you and Q4 for them.

Thinking tokens are ordinary output tokens. They are billed at the output price, even when the app shows you only a summary or nothing at all.

Most modern models will keep that thinking in every later turn of the conversation.

That is an additional 2,100 tokens you carry around, for output you don’t even see.

Ok, that makes sense.

Want me to add a footnote that explains the gap?

All of this would be painful (and prohibitively expensive) without caching.

In practice, the provider keeps your conversation in its memory for a few minutes.

When the next request starts with exactly the same tokens, that part is a cache hit.

Yes, then move on to the spend section.

Added the footnote and drafted spend, with a table by category.

Looks good.

I'll leave it there unless you want more.

The striped blocks are hits. On Claude Sonnet 5.5, a cache read costs 0.05x the normal input price.

Only what is new since the last request gets written to cache, at 1.25x.

The catch: cache has a short lifetime. For Anthropic, it is 5 minutes , and every hit resets the clock, so it stays warm while you are replying.

Then you go get a coffee…

You come back and ask where you were.

The cache is gone, so the whole thing is processed and written to cache again at 1.25x the price.

That request costs ~ 15 times more than the one before the coffee break.

Back. Where were we?

Headcount and spend are drafted, with the travel footnote. Incidents is next.

The cache covers everything from the top of the prompt down to the first token that differs.

Since tools are defined at the very top, changing them invalidates the entire cache .

You connect Slack in the middle of the session. Its tool definitions land at the top of the prompt, and your cache is reset.

You ask it for a complex report. The assistant calls a tool, gets the result, and calls another one.

Each step is a separate request, and each one re-sends everything before it plus the latest tool result.

Draft the incidents section from the tracker and the team's weekly updates.

Searched Drive for Q3 incidents

Read Incident tracker Q3.xlsx

Read 12 weekly updates

Drafted in the doc: 11 incidents, two customer-facing. Both trace back to the July billing migration.

You sent one message and the model received 4 requests.

The weekly updates it read are now the biggest block in the prompt.

When an assistant works through your files, tool results are where the context goes.

So far the panel has been zoomed in. This is the same conversation drawn against a 200,000-token context size. This is the hard limit on how much the model can read in one request.

Newer models go up to a million tokens.

An afternoon of report work later, reading spreadsheets, email threads and PDFs, the prompt has crept up to the dashed line, the compaction threshold.

Every document it read is still in there, sent again on every request.

An afternoon of report work later

Read Budget Q3.xlsx

Read Hiring plan.docx

Edited the report

Read 9 email threads

Searched Drive for board notes

Read Board deck Q3.pdf

Read #ops-incidents in Slack

Read Vendor contract.pdf

Read comments on the draft

Read the full expense export

When the context crosses that threshold, the assistant compacts it.

The model writes a summary of the conversation so far, and the app replaces the older turns with that summary.

Tools and the system prompt stay where they are, and only the most recent messages survive next to the summary.

Conversation compacted

Most assistants will do this automatically before the window fills.

In Claude Code, the /compact command triggers it manually.

The chat history isn’t impacted, so the UI lies to you. The model no longer has any of it. All it has is a 3,400-token summary of what happened.

You ask what the Q2 report said about the vendor contract.

The summary kept the conclusion and dropped the text, so the model can tell you what it decided back then but not what the report said.

What did the Q2 report say about the vendor contract?

I only have a summary of that part now: Q2 flagged the renewal as a risk. Can you paste that section again?

The context window is the only memory the model has. Everything in it is paid for again on every request, and whatever gets compacted out is gone for the model while it stays on your screen.

https://blog.raed.dev/posts/proton-loser.markdown:
I’ve been paying for Proton for many years, and it’s what I recommend when someone asks how to get off Gmail. This week 404 Media published an investigation into how Proton’s leadership is pushing AI inside the company. The detail that made the rounds came from the security Slack channel: an engineer asked for a few days to pentest new code before shipping it, and CEO Andy Yen answered that it was “bullshit and loser thinking” , then told the team to stop lovingly handcrafting code and use AI more.

For the first time, I’m not sure I’d still recommend them.

A lot of the reactions treat this as an AI story, as if any AI-written code poisons the well, and I think that misses the point. Engineers using AI to write code is the new norm. It’s fine as long as there are guardrails around it: someone reviews what the model produced, it gets tested, and someone is accountable for what ships .

What the reporting describes is a CEO telling an engineer, in front of colleagues, that raising a security concern was “loser thinking” . Staff were told their AI usage could decide whether they kept their jobs , and when that plan was dropped after it leaked, Yen said it had already served its purpose . None of this is about AI. Plenty of companies are rolling out coding agents right now without humiliating anyone, so if Proton can’t, the problem sits with its leadership.

## The tradeoff Proton can’t make

For most companies, trading some caution for speed is a reasonable call. Proton is a privacy company, though, and what its users pay for is the confidence that the people building it are careful. Shipping slowly and carefully is part of what they’re selling. A bad release from a B2B vendor can be catastrophic , but for a company like Proton, a bug that exposes users’ mail would be fatal.

One of the employees defending the company on Reddit added some context that was meant to help: Yen was fine with pentesting, as long as it didn’t slow down the pipeline.

This is one of a few employees pretending to courageously dissent, but in reality agreeing with the official corporate line. It reads like astroturfing and a clumsy attempt at crisis management. No employee who shared on Reddit disagrees with how things were handled or with where the company is going.

Beyond the clumsiness, it shows a leadership that now treats the constraints that made Proton worth paying for as the thing slowing it down.

I’d like to keep recommending Proton, but that depends on the engineer asking for a few more days of testing still winning the argument against a leadership obsessed with velocity and arbitrary release dates.
